candidates.attacker_control: A remote network peer that can reach the name server's listening port (default 9876) fully controls the RemotingCommand: request code 318 (UPDATE_NAMESRV_CONFIG), body bytes, and therefore all property names/values. No credential, signature, or ACL hook is involved on the name server (ACL/RPC hooks are registered only by BrokerController.java:500-540; namesrv registers none, and DefaultRequestProcessor.rejectRequest() always returns false).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified the guard text and that `configStorePathName` appears exactly once in the entire repository (only at the guard itself), so it can never match a setter; verified NamesrvConfig's full field/setter list and that `configStorePath` is the real property and the registered store-path field; verified Configuration.update applies all request properties via properties2Object (not just pre-existing keys) and persists unconditionally; verified MixAll.string2File writes to the resolved store path and not a sandboxed directory; verified the namesrv registers no RPCHook/AccessValidator (only BrokerController registers ACL hooks) and that the name-server port is used by ordinary clients, making code 318 pre-auth reachable; verified ClusterTestRequestProcessor inherits the same updateConfig; verified the broker does not share the primitive (BrokerConfig has no configStorePath field and BrokerController.java:218-222 uses a fixed BrokerPathConfigHelper.getBrokerConfigPath()), and that no Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder/FilterServerManager exists in this snapshot, so no direct shell-execution claim is made.
candidates.impact: Unauthenticated arbitrary-path file write/overwrite on the host running the NameServer, executed with the name-server process's privileges and with partially attacker-controlled content. Practical effects: overwrite or corrupt any file writable by that user (including the configuration file used at startup), persist attacker-chosen name-server settings such as `rocketmqHome` (not guarded either) which selects the logback configuration file loaded at next startup (NamesrvStartup.java:119) and `configStorePath` itself (NamesrvStartup.java:94 sets it from the -c file), and cause persistent denial of service. Because Properties escapes can inject additional lines, the primitive may support broader content control on some deployment layouts, creating a plausible secondary path to code execution where the service writes to files that are later executed or parsed by other system components; that escalation is a hypothesis, not established here.
candidates.prerequisites: TCP reachability to the NameServer port (the port is client-facing: producers/consumers resolve routes through it, so any cluster client or adjacent network host can reach it); default name-server code path without authentication; for the file-write impact, a target path that is writable by the name-server process user (impact is highest when the service runs as root, as commonly deployed in containers).
candidates.root_cause: DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig rejects only properties named `kvConfigPath` and `configStorePathName` (DefaultRequestProcessor.java:584). No config object defines a `configStorePathName` property: NamesrvConfig defines `configStorePath` (NamesrvConfig.java:34, getter/setter 79-85), so that half of the guard is dead code. NamesrvController.java:73 had already registered `namesrvConfig.configStorePath` as the Configuration store path (`setStorePathFromConfig(this.namesrvConfig, "configStorePath")`), therefore a request that sets `configStorePath` changes the target of Configuration.persist().
candidates.title: Unauthenticated NameServer config update allows arbitrary-path file write because the config-path guard checks a non-existent property name
candidates.trace: 1) NamesrvController.registerProcessor installs DefaultRequestProcessor as the default processor (NamesrvController.java:132-140), and any unrecognized code falls through to it (NettyRemotingAbstract.java:192-197); code 318 is explicitly dispatched at DefaultRequestProcessor.java:130-131. 2) updateConfig parses the attacker body with MixAll.string2Properties (283-294, java.util.Properties.load) and applies the guard at line 584; because `configStorePathName` matches no field/setter, `configStorePath=<attacker path>` passes. 3) Configuration.update (Configuration.java:175-199) calls MixAll.properties2Object for each registered config object (MixAll.java:322-360), which reflectively invokes NamesrvConfig.setConfigStorePath (NamesrvConfig.java:83) and stores the attacker string. 4) update() then calls persist() (Configuration.java:198, 201-217); getStorePath() (146-169) returns the bound field value (the attacker's path, since NamesrvController.java:73 set storePathFromConfig for exactly that field), and MixAll.string2File (146-162) writes the config dump, creating parent directories and .tmp/.bak siblings. 5) The written content is produced by getAllConfigsInternal/properties2String (Configuration.java:259-277; MixAll.java:273-281), which emits values verbatim; values entered with Java properties escapes (e.g. a two-character backslash-n) are unescaped into real newlines by Properties.load and re-emitted unescaped, so attacker-set values can introduce additional lines into the file.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed, so the write was not observed at runtime; the existence of writable, high-impact target paths depends on deployment (user privileges, container/root usage) and was not confirmed. The newline-injection content-control detail is inferred from java.util.Properties.load/properties2String semantics, not runtime-tested. The secondary code-execution escalation (e.g. influencing logback/Joran configuration at next startup, or overwriting files later executed) is deployment-dependent and not proven. Impact description deliberately avoids payloads.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-73 External Control of File Name or Path combined with CWE-306 Missing Authentication for Critical Function (broken denylist on a network-reachable config update)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 870 model-visible files, no exclusions (binary-like/oversize/symlink/sensitive-name filters removed none). P1 index: 840 files indexed, 30 source files missing from the index, 335 files parsed, 11,894 symbols and 28,185 syntax-level edges, with no control-flow, no data-flow, and no semantic resolution; omitted/unparsed areas were not assumed reviewed. Files inspected directly: root pom.xml (version 4.9.6, fastjson/netty properties), namesrv processor/controller/startup (DefaultRequestProcessor incl. full updateConfig and dispatch, ClusterTestRequestProcessor, NamesrvController, NamesrvStartup), common Configuration, MixAll (string/properties/object conversions and file helpers), NamesrvConfig, RequestCode, remoting NettyRemotingAbstract dispatch and RemotingCommand decode, broker BrokerController Configuration/ACL-hook setup, AdminBrokerProcessor updateBrokerConfig/getBrokerConfig, BrokerPathConfigHelper, BrokerConfig field searches. Repo-wide text sweeps: configStorePath/configStorePathName, Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder, FilterServer, AccessValidator/registerServerRPCHook, CVE, updateConfig tests. Not reviewed in depth: client module internals, store engine internals, tools/srvutil, DLedger, TLS/FileWatchService, ACL plain-permission internals, tests, and non-Java docs/scripts.
limitations: No code, tests, or scanners were executed; reachability and file-write behavior are based on source reasoning plus syntactic index navigation, not runtime confirmation.

The P1 index is partial: only 335 of 731 Java files parsed, 30 source files absent from the index, and no data-flow/control-flow/Spring enforcement analysis, so other vulnerable paths could exist outside what was inspected.

The candidate's impact depends on deployment specifics that cannot be verified from source alone: name-server port exposure, process user/privileges, and whether any writable target path has security-relevant consumers.
Newline/escape-based content control in the written file is inferred from java.util.Properties and MixAll semantics and was not demonstrated at runtime.
Dependency versions (netty, logback, fastjson) were not matched against vulnerability data, as external lookups are out of scope for this run.

rejected_leads.lead: Broker AdminBrokerProcessor.updateBrokerConfig (broker/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/broker/processor/AdminBrokerProcessor.java:514-548) accepts arbitrary properties without any denylist when ACL is disabled (default), so a remote client can alter broker config (e.g. brokerPermission).
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness but no arbitrary-path primitive: BrokerConfig has no configStorePath field (repo-wide search), and BrokerController.java:218-222 builds its Configuration with the fixed BrokerPathConfigHelper.getBrokerConfigPath(), so persist() cannot be redirected. The historical filter-server shell chain is absent (no FilterServerManager/mqfiltersrv code, no Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder anywhere). Selected lead is strictly stronger.

rejected_leads.lead: Unauthenticated name server KV config operations (PUT_KV_CONFIG/GET_KV_CONFIG/DELETE_KV_CONFIG, DefaultRequestProcessor.java:145-200) let any client read/write/delete KV entries.
rejected_leads.reason: These operate on the configured kvConfigPath, and that property name is correctly blocked by the guard (line 584), so no arbitrary-path write was found; behavior is largely by design for the name server in this version. Not retained as the primary candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: RemotingCommand JSON header decoding with fastjson (RemotingCommand.java:184-201, pom.xml:107 uses fastjson 1.2.69_noneautotype).
rejected_leads.reason: The dependency is the project's no-autotype build and no autoType/gadget configuration was found in source; no evidence of an exploitable deserialization path was established. Not claimed.

rejected_leads.lead: Plain ACL permission manager files/writes (acl/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/acl/plain/PlainPermissionManager.java) and file-based ACL import paths.
rejected_leads.reason: ACL is opt-in and broker-only (BrokerConfig.isAclEnable default false; BrokerController.java:500-515), and this code was not deeply reviewed; no concrete, source-verifiable vulnerability with comparable impact was identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Dependency-level exposure (netty 4.1.65.Final at pom.xml:105, logback/logging module, fastjson).
rejected_leads.reason: No CVE/version databases are available in this run and no source-level exploitation path was established; treated as an unverified hardening observation, not a finding.

summary: Reviewed the Apache RocketMQ 4.9.6 snapshot (pom.xml:32), focusing on remotely reachable config-update/admin handlers and the shared Configuration/MixAll config-persistence primitives. One candidate submitted: the name server's unauthenticated UPDATE_NAMESRV_CONFIG handler (code 318) attempts to forbid changing config-file paths but checks a property name that does not exist anywhere in the tree (`configStorePathName`), so a remote client can set `configStorePath`; because NamesrvController bound that same field as the Configuration store path, the subsequent persist() writes the name-server config dump to an attacker-chosen filesystem path with attacker-influenced values. Other leads (broker updateBrokerConfig without denylist, unauthenticated KV writes, fastjson/netty versions, ACL internals) were checked and rejected as weaker or unevidenced; they are listed as rejected leads.
